title: İmam bayıldı
subtitle: Turkish slow-braised aubergines stuffed with onion, tomato, and garlic
excerpt: Imam bayildi is a Turkish classic: whole aubergines are slit open and packed with a soft, fragrant mixture of onion, tomato, and garlic, then braised slowly in olive oil until meltingly tender. It is a dish of concentrated sweetness and is eaten at room temperature. The name means the imam fainted.
sourceNotes: A famous dish of Turkish cuisine with a playful name: legend says the imam fainted with pleasure (or at the cost of the olive oil) when he first tasted it. It is eaten across Turkey and in Greek cooking as well.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best made a day ahead. Serve at room temperature; reheating is optional.

content.text: Imam bayildi is the kind of dish that rewards patience. The aubergines need slow, gentle heat to collapse into softness without burning, and the stuffing needs time to cook down to a sweet, jammy mass before it goes in. Rush either stage and you lose something essential.
The dish is eaten at room temperature, which means it can be made hours or even a day in advance. Cold from the fridge it is less good; let it come back to room temperature before serving.
Olive oil is the cooking medium and you need to use it generously. The aubergines absorb a remarkable amount; this is how they become so yielding and flavourful.

Peel the aubergines in alternating strips to create a striped effect. Make a deep slit lengthways down each one, from about 2 cm below the stem to 2 cm from the base, without cutting all the way through. Rub salt into the slit and the cut surfaces. Set aside on a plate for 20 minutes, then pat dry with kitchen paper.

Heat 80 ml of olive oil in the frying pan over medium-low heat. Add the sliced onions and cook very slowly for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until completely soft and golden. Add the garlic and cook for 5 more minutes. Add the tomatoes, parsley, sugar, and salt. Cook for 10 minutes until the tomatoes have softened and the mixture is thick. Set aside to cool slightly.

Preheat the oven to 180 C. Heat the remaining olive oil in a heavy ovenproof casserole over medium heat. Brown the aubergines gently on all sides for about 4 minutes. Remove them and spoon the stuffing generously into each slit. Arrange them stuffed-side up in the casserole. Mix the hot water, olive oil, and lemon juice together and pour around the aubergines. Cover tightly and braise in the oven for 45 to 55 minutes until the aubergines are very tender and have collapsed. Leave to cool to room temperature in the pot.

rows.symptom: Aubergines still firm after cooking time
rows.cause: Oven not hot enough or pot not sealed
rows.fix: Check the pot lid fits tightly. Add another 100 ml of hot water and cook for a further 20 minutes.
Cook the stuffing until almost all liquid has gone before filling the aubergines; excess moisture makes it soggy.
Salt for the full 20 minutes and pat very dry before cooking.

content.text: Some versions add a pinch of allspice or cinnamon to the stuffing. For a sharper result, use a tablespoon of pomegranate syrup in place of the lemon juice in the braising liquid. Courgettes can be stuffed and cooked in the same way.
Imam bayildi is always better the next day. Cook it completely, then let it cool in the pot and refrigerate. Remove from the fridge 1 hour before serving to bring it back to room temperature.

Imam bayildi is both Turkish and Greek in heritage; versions of it appear across the eastern Mediterranean. In Turkey it is served as a meze, a starter, or a main course depending on the context. It is best in late summer when both aubergines and tomatoes are at their peak.
